name: Telebit
popularity: Very low on its own git host: 2 stars, 1 fork, 1 watcher on git.coolaj86.com (a self-hosted Gitea, not GitHub, so visibility/discoverability is minimal). No GitHub mirror with meaningful star count found. Single-maintainer project (AJ ONeal / coolaj86) promoted mainly via his own blog/talks.
maturity: Surprisingly still receiving commits: latest commit 2025-10-26 (version bump to v0.20.251025), 523 commits total on the 'stable' branch, 72 tags. However most feature work (README, lib, client code) dates to 2018-2019; recent commits look like small maintenance/packaging bumps rather than active feature development. Hosted service (telebit.cloud) still appears to be up. Single maintainer is a red flag for long-term reliability, and the project is not widely known/adopted.
client_requirements: Single CLI/binary install via `curl https://get.telebit.io/ | bash` (installs a Node.js-based client). No TUN/TAP interface; no root/admin required for basic `telebit http <port>` usage (uses application-layer HTTPS/TLS tunneling, not a VPN). Requires device 'claiming' via email confirmation, which adds friction for fully automated/headless provisioning.
server_requirements: Server source code is available in the same JS repo (it's a combined client+server Node.js codebase), so self-hosting is technically possible, though docs/support for running your own server independently of telebit.cloud are thin and mostly undocumented/community-figured-out. It is fundamentally a Node.js daemon; no separate first-class REST/control-plane API is documented for programmatic tunnel registration — provisioning is designed around the email-claim CLI flow, not an API you'd call from a backend.
has_programmable_api: false (or unclear) — JavaScript/Node.js codebase; no documented external HTTP API for registering tunnels programmatically. The Node.js server library could theoretically be embedded/imported into another Node app, but there's no supported SvelteKit-callable REST control-plane.
viability_notes: Client constraint is fine (simple CLI, no TUN/root), and it's genuinely open source with a permissive MIT license, but the ecosystem is essentially a single-maintainer side project with negligible adoption, poor documentation for self-hosting, and no clean programmatic API for our SvelteKit backend to hit. Not dead, but too obscure/fragile to build on with confidence.

name: tunnel.pyjam.as
license: Open source (permissive; per awesome-tunneling listing) — exact SPDX not independently confirmed beyond a LICENSE file present in repo
popularity: Very low visibility: hosted on GitLab (not GitHub), no star/fork counts surfaced in normal search; essentially a personal/small project by a single author (Asbjørn Kofoed-Nielsen). Not a widely adopted tool.
maturity: Repo exists with a CI pipeline (recent commit 'Remove javascript from index.html'), so it isn't completely abandoned, but it's a small, low-traffic project with no release/version cadence visible. Effectively a single-maintainer service.
client_requirements: FAILS the client constraint outright: per the awesome-tunneling list, tunnel.pyjam.as has 'No custom client; uses WireGuard directly instead.' That means the client must set up a WireGuard interface (a VPN kernel/userspace network interface), which is exactly the TUN/TAP-style requirement we must avoid, and typically needs elevated privileges to configure.
server_requirements: Server source available (Python, on GitLab). No separate documented REST/control-plane API for third-party backends to call — it's WireGuard-config driven.
has_programmable_api: false — it's a WireGuard config generator/service, not an HTTP API for tunnel registration from an external app.
viability_notes: Hard-fails our primary constraint because it relies on the client running WireGuard (a VPN network interface) rather than a simple binary/CLI, and it also lacks any programmable HTTP control-plane. Low adoption and single-maintainer status compound the risk. Not viable for our use case.

name: SSH-J.com
license: Not clearly published as a distinct client/server library license — this is essentially a public hosted SSH server configuration/service, not a packaged software project with its own release artifacts.
language: N/A — it is a public, anonymous SSH jump/port-forwarding server (based on dropbear SSH), not a distributable client or server codebase we would deploy ourselves.
popularity: No GitHub stars/forks (Bitbucket-hosted, single small repo). Known within the awesome-tunneling / self-hosting community as a free public utility, but not a software project with adoption metrics — it's a single public instance, also reachable over Tor onion service.
maturity: Appears to be a long-running personal hosted service by ValdikSS (also accessible via Tor onion), still live per its landing page (ssh-j.com), but has essentially no development activity to speak of — it's a static SSH server config, not actively 'released' software. Fundamentally a single operator's hosted service — classic bus-factor/abandonment risk (if the operator stops hosting it, the service disappears).
client_requirements: Explicitly 'No software, no registration' — just an ordinary SSH client (`ssh -R ...`), which every OS already ships. This is arguably the simplest possible client requirement: no custom binary, no TUN/TAP, no admin/root needed to run `ssh -R`. Excellent fit for the client-side constraint.
server_requirements: There is no server source code to self-host — SSH-J.com IS the server, run by a third party (ValdikSS) as a public shared multi-tenant service, limited to 50 exposed ports/username, intended only for SSH-to-SSH forwarding (they explicitly discourage exposing raw non-SSH public ports). We cannot host our own instance from published source, and there is no HTTP/REST control-plane at all — it's raw SSH port-forwarding semantics only.
server_language: N/A (dropbear SSH server, C, but not really an installable 'product' — it's a specific person's server configuration)
has_programmable_api: false — no API of any kind; it's raw `ssh -R`/`-J` semantics with no control-plane, and we don't control or host the server ourselves.
viability_notes: Client side is ideal (plain ssh, zero install), but this fails our other hard requirement: it's a third-party shared public service with no self-hostable server source and zero programmatic API — we cannot register/manage tunnels from our own backend, and we can't run 'our own' server binary since the software isn't really packaged for redistribution. Not usable for our architecture.

name: Greenhouse
popularity: Minimal: 0 stars, 0 forks, 2 watchers on its self-hosted Gitea instance (git.sequentialread.com). Niche project by a solo developer ('forest'/SequentialRead), not tracked on GitHub, no meaningful adoption signal found.
maturity: Effectively abandoned/stalled: last substantive activity was years ago (README last updated ~5 years ago per commit history, a security doc updated ~3 years ago), and per the awesome-tunneling list itself: 'The hosted service (greenhouse.server.garden) is currently unavailable and the project appears unmaintained (last activity 2023).' Explicit red flag of a dead hosted service and single-maintainer abandonment.
client_requirements: Designed to be a lightweight port-forwarding client with automatic HTTPS ('least-authority' design so the service never holds your TLS private keys), which in principle sounds admin-free, but with the project dead and hosted service down, this is moot — there is no functioning client/server pairing to evaluate in practice today.
server_requirements: Full server source is available (Go, self-hostable), including an admin panel with token-based API keys (public_api.go, threshold_provisioning_service.go) suggesting some HTTP-based control API existed for the hosted alpha/beta service, but there's no current documentation, it's unmaintained, and the hosted reference instance is down — reviving/self-hosting it would require significant unsupported reverse-engineering effort.
has_programmable_api: Possibly true historically (Go) — code includes a 'public_api.go' and multiple API tokens per the commit history — but undocumented, unmaintained, and unverifiable as currently working.
viability_notes: Interesting design goals (least-authority, no custom client TLS key handoff) but the project and its hosted service are dead, it's a single-maintainer effort with zero community adoption, and any API surface is undocumented and unmaintained. Not a safe foundation to build production tunneling on.

name: frp
popularity: Extremely popular: 109.5k GitHub stars, 15.2k forks, 1.6k watchers, 1,524+ commits. One of the most widely used open-source reverse-proxy/tunnel tools; has an active related-projects ecosystem (gofrp/plugin, gofrp/tiny-frpc), CI badges, GitHub Sponsors, and corporate sponsors (JetBrains, RapidProxy, Olares). Very strong, long-standing adoption signal.
maturity: Actively maintained: dev branch under continuous development, recent feature-gate/experimental-feature system documented (ALPHA/BETA/GA lifecycle), ongoing releases via GitHub Releases and CircleCI. No abandonment red flags — large contributor base, not single-maintainer dependent for day-to-day operation despite fatedier being lead.
client_requirements: Single static Go binary (frpc) — no TUN/TAP, no admin/root required for standard TCP/HTTP/HTTPS proxying (root only needed if binding to privileged ports <1024, same as any normal server software). Config-file driven (TOML) but can also be driven via CLI flags/env vars. There's also a 'tiny-frpc' variant (~3.5MB) for constrained devices. Overall this is an excellent, simple client story.
server_requirements: Full server (frps) source code available in the same repo (Go). frps does expose an HTTP-based Admin API / Dashboard (documented in the frp docs, e.g. `/api/*` endpoints for reload, proxy status, server info) that can be queried, though it's primarily geared toward admin/monitoring and reload-of-config rather than a full first-class 'create tunnel' REST resource-oriented API for provisioning arbitrary tunnels at runtime without config. Frp's typical model is: client authenticates with a token and requests proxies itself (proxies are largely declared in the frpc config, though frpc also has features for env-var and dynamic config, and there's an admin API on the client side too). It's more 'config/token-driven binary with a monitoring/admin HTTP API' than a full programmatic-tunnel-creation REST API, but it is scriptable and self-hostable, and the wire protocol/API is documented enough that a backend could plausibly automate it (e.g., by templating frpc config and restarting/reloading, or via its client admin API).
has_programmable_api: Partially true — Go; frps/frpc expose an HTTP Admin API (dashboard, reload, proxy/traffic stats) documented in frp's docs, and frpc supports config reload without restart. It is not a purpose-built 'POST /tunnels' REST API for on-demand tunnel registration, but the admin API + reload mechanism + token auth model gives a workable path to drive it programmatically from a backend.
viability_notes: Best-in-class maturity, adoption, and client simplicity (single static Go binary, no TUN/root) make frp a very strong candidate; the main gap versus a 'true' JS/TS control-plane API is that tunnel provisioning is more config/reload-oriented than resource-style REST, requiring us to write glue code (config templating + reload, or driving the admin API) rather than calling a clean 'create tunnel' endpoint. Still a top pick given its maturity and self-hostability.

name: ngrok 1.0
popularity: 24.4k GitHub stars, 4.3k forks — historically very popular (2013-2016 era, the tool that essentially popularized this whole category), but that popularity is legacy/historical rather than current.
maturity: Explicitly dead as an open-source project: GitHub shows 'This repository was archived by the owner on Jun 3, 2024. It is now read-only,' and the README states plainly: 'This is the GitHub repository for the old v1 version of ngrok which was actively developed from 2013-2016... This repository is archived: ngrok v1 is no longer developed, supported or maintained.' The commercial ngrok 2.0+ service continues, but that is closed-source with its own API/SDKs (ngrok-go, ngrok-javascript, ngrok-python, etc.) — a different product entirely from this archived open-source repo.
client_requirements: N/A for our purposes — codebase is unmaintained/archived and the original hosted ngrokd service this client talked to is long gone; self-hosting v1 today would require reviving 8+ year old Go code with no support.
server_requirements: Source (ngrokd) is technically available in the archived repo (Go), so in theory it could be self-hosted/forked, but there is zero ongoing maintenance, no security patching, and no programmable control-plane API documented for v1.
has_programmable_api: false for this v1 codebase — no documented control-plane API; the JS/Python/Go/Rust/Java 'agent SDKs' mentioned on the archived README belong to the separate, closed-source ngrok 2.0+ commercial product, not this repo.
viability_notes: Explicitly archived/abandoned by its own maintainer in favor of a closed-source commercial successor — a clear-cut dead project despite its large historical star count. Not viable to build on; the only 'API' ecosystem (ngrok agent SDKs) belongs to the commercial closed-source ngrok, which is out of scope since we need open source.

name: Pangolin
license: Dual-licensed: AGPL-3.0 (open source) and Fossorial Commercial License (for commercial use cases)
language: TypeScript / Next.js (server + dashboard); companion client 'newt' is Go
popularity: 22.8k GitHub stars, 786 forks, 71 watchers, 8,469+ commits — very actively developed and increasingly popular self-hosted SASE/zero-trust platform. Its client connector 'newt' has its own repo with 909 stars / 87 forks. Explicitly recommended in the awesome-tunneling README as one of two 'production ready' self-hosted options (alongside frp).
maturity: Very actively maintained: huge, continuously growing commit history (8,469 commits), current feature work includes an 'AI Gateway,' recent architecture docs, and an official hosted Pangolin Cloud offering alongside self-hosting — strong signal of ongoing investment, not a single-maintainer side project (fosrl org, commercial backing).
client_requirements: The client connector, 'newt,' is a single static Go binary (get-newt.sh install script; also packaged for Windows via Inno Setup, Nix flake, Docker). Critically, newt implements WireGuard fully in userspace via netstack (gVisor's userspace TCP/IP stack) rather than creating a kernel TUN/TAP device — per its own README: 'it will use the information encoded (endpoint, public key) to bring up a WireGuard tunnel using netstack... fully in user space.' This means no OS-level TUN/TAP interface and no admin/root privileges are required to run it — it registers with the Pangolin server over HTTP+WebSocket using an ID/secret, a good fit for our constraint.
server_requirements: Full server source available (TypeScript/Next.js control plane + Go 'Gerbil' WireGuard exit-node component), self-hostable via Docker Compose. Newt registers with Pangolin via plain HTTP requests to get a session token, then holds a WebSocket for control messages — i.e., there IS a documented HTTP+WebSocket control-plane protocol between client and server, though the full public developer-facing REST API surface for third-party backends (e.g., 'create site/resource via our own code') would need confirming against docs.pangolin.net, but the architecture (identity, sites, resources, clients all as first-class managed objects in a Next.js/TypeScript control plane) strongly suggests a workable admin API exists for programmatic registration.
server_language: TypeScript (Next.js control plane), Go (Gerbil exit-node / WireGuard component)
has_programmable_api: Likely true — TypeScript; Pangolin's control plane is a TypeScript/Next.js app with organized resources (sites, resources, clients, identity/access) and a documented registration handshake (HTTP session token + WebSocket control channel) used by the newt client itself, implying an internal REST/WS API that a SvelteKit backend could potentially call or emulate, though full public API docs would need direct verification for a supported 'register tunnel' surface.
viability_notes: Best overall fit: hosted server binary/Docker deployment is expected and well-documented, the client (newt) is a single Go binary using userspace WireGuard (no TUN/TAP, no root) satisfying our hardest constraint, and the control plane is TypeScript with an HTTP+WebSocket registration protocol that aligns closely with 'hittable control-plane from our SvelteKit backend.' Very active development and strong adoption reduce abandonment risk versus the other candidates. Top pick.

name: chisel
popularity: 16.5k GitHub stars, 1.6k forks, 207 watchers, 261 commits. Well-established, widely used utility (also packaged for Fedora/EPEL, Docker Hub + GHCR images), commonly cited as an ngrok/SSH-tunnel alternative.
maturity: Actively maintained: recent changelog entries describe substantive v1.12 changes (SOCKS5 authfile enforcement, SHA256 fingerprint requirements, graceful shutdown, UDP connection caps, Go 1.27.0 builds, updated x/crypto/ssh to address a CVE) — clear evidence of an actively developed, security-conscious release cadence, not a stalled project. Single primary maintainer (Jaime Pillora) but healthy release/issue activity.
client_requirements: Single static Go binary combining both client and server (`chisel client`, `chisel server`); no TUN/TAP interface, no admin/root required for typical use (transports TCP/UDP over HTTP secured via SSH protocol under the hood, entirely in userspace). Trivial install via `curl .../chisel! | bash`, Docker, `go install`, or OS packages. Excellent fit for the client constraint — arguably as simple as it gets.
server_requirements: Full source available (single Go repo, MIT licensed); the 'chisel server' binary is what we'd host. However, it is fundamentally a CLI/flag-driven binary (e.g., `chisel server --port $PORT --backend ...`) with no HTTP REST control-plane / admin API of its own for creating or managing tunnels at runtime — tunnels are established by clients connecting and requesting specific remote forwards via the CLI/protocol, not via a management API we'd call from a backend. There's no separate provisioning API to hit; any orchestration (e.g., generating per-user auth tokens via `--authfile`, spawning/killing server processes) would have to be built by us around the binary.
has_programmable_api: false as a control-plane — Go source is embeddable as a library (chisel is importable as a Go package, e.g., github.com/jpillora/chisel/server), which is useful if our backend were Go, but there's no JS/TS/HTTP-native control-plane API; from a SvelteKit backend we would only be able to shell out to / manage the binary and its authfile/config, not call a REST API to register tunnels.
viability_notes: Chisel is mature, popular, and has by far the simplest possible client (single static binary, zero TUN/root), making it a very strong operational fit; the downside relative to Pangolin is the total lack of any HTTP/TS control-plane — we'd have to build our own glue (authfile management, process control) around a config/CLI-driven binary rather than calling an API. Solid fallback if Pangolin's control plane doesn't pan out.
